newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine says feels snubbed financially by the West.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine says feels snubbed financially by the West.

text.p: Ukraine, for years a favoured child of the West, made clear this week it feels snubbed after two prospects for financial aid fell through.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has delayed a multi-billion-dollar loan to Ukraine and the Group of Seven industrialised nations (G7) decided to give less than Kiev expected to shut down Chernobyl.
The $2.5 to $3 billion Extended Fund Facility IMF loan, to succeed a $867 million stand-by deal that expired in February, has been held up because of Ukraine's delay in meeting some 41 conditions.
Key on the list is the budget, which was due to get a final reading in parliament only late on Thursday, a record delay in passing a budget since Kiev won independence six years ago.
Last weekend in Denver, the G7 allocated $300 million to fix the ruined fourth reactor at Chernobyl. The amount fell short of the $750 million Kiev wanted.

"Declarations are one thing but financial aid is another, especially where Chernobyl is concerned," Yevhen Kushnaryov, head of President Leonid Kuchma's administration, said on Thursday. "Nothing will happen with only words. Money should be given to meet the promises to close the plant in 2000."
Yevhen Kushnaryov, head of Kuchma's administration, also accused the IMF of helping Ukrainian leftist forces by not giving final agreement to the loan.

"We think the IMF must take the political situation in modern Ukraine into account," he said. "Non-delivery of the aid works in favour of leftist forces because it makes the political and social situation worse...The IMF is failing to see the difficulties of legally implementing economic reforms through parliament."

Kuchma, who returned on Wednesday from meeting IMF officials in New York, was quoted by Ukrainian news agencies as slamming the IMF. He said IMF reluctance was pushing Ukraine back into the arms of the Kremlin.

"It seems the authors of the IMF's decisions and Ukrainian leftists stand on the same side of the barricades, willing to return Ukraine to the Soviet Union," Kuchma was quoted as telling leaders of the American-Ukrainian community.
"The first ones block the adoption of the budget, so the second one then suspends the credit, which is needed for Ukraine's fiscal balance," he said.
A poll published this week by the respected Den daily showed Communists were the most popular party in Ukraine with 11 percent, followed by national democrats with 10 percent.
Another Den poll showed 51 percent of Ukrainians regretted the 1991 break-up of the Soviet superpower.
Leftists in parliament often accuse the government of making Ukraine a "slave" to international financial institutions.
Ukraine is the third largest recipient of U.S. aid after Israel and Egypt, receiving $300 million this year.
Since launching reforms in 1994, Ukraine has received several billion dollars from the IMF and the World Bank.

Last week, Kuchma's top economic aide, Valery Lytvytsky, said the IMF should take "the same aproach towards Ukraine as it used to take towards Russia." That includes accounting for the political situation and possible steps by Communists and their allies.
But some observers in Kiev disagreed.
"Ukraine keeps changing the figure for Chernobyl. God knows which one was correct and final," Vyacheslav Pikhovshek, head of the Centre for Independent Political Research, said.
"The IMF cannot change its basic principle because of a single country. The 'left argument' is unlikely to work as Russia has already used it far too often," he added.
